items.prompt: An apple's sweet flesh is safe to eat, yet its seeds contain a mild toxin. Why put a toxin only in the seed?

options.label: The toxin is a mistake left over from an earlier stage of the fruit's growth
options.feedback: The toxin is produced specifically inside the seed's own tissue, in a location too precise to be an accidental leftover from some earlier, unrelated stage.

options.label: The toxin keeps the flesh from rotting before an animal finds it
options.feedback: The toxin sits inside the seed itself, not spread through the surrounding flesh, so it cannot be what is protecting the flesh from decay.

options.label: The sweet flesh is meant to be eaten and carried off, but the embryo inside the seed still needs protection from being chewed and destroyed along with it
options.feedback: An animal that bites all the way through a seed rather than swallowing it whole would crush the embryo, so a deterrent kept inside the seed discourages exactly that, while the flesh outside remains perfectly safe to eat.

options.label: The toxin is only dangerous to insects, never to a larger animal
options.feedback: The toxin found in fruit seeds like these can affect animals as well as insects if enough is consumed; its main role is deterring the seed itself from being chewed, whatever size the animal is.

items.ok_line: Reward in the flesh, warning in the seed.
items.ko_line: The plant wants the flesh eaten but the seed left whole. What would placing a deterrent specifically inside the seed achieve?
items.exp_title: A warning kept exactly where it is needed
items.exp_text: A fruit's flesh is built to be found and eaten so its seeds can travel inside the animal that swallows it, but that only works if the seed itself survives the trip unharmed. Putting a bitter or toxic compound specifically inside the seed's own tissue discourages an animal from biting down and chewing through it, while leaving the surrounding flesh perfectly safe and appealing. The reward and the warning sit in two different places for two different reasons.

items.prompt: Why does a horse chestnut or a durian wrap its seed in a hard, spiky outer husk?

options.label: The spines make the husk difficult and painful for a ground animal to bite into or carry off before the seed inside is ready
options.feedback: A mouth or paw closing around a husk covered in sharp spines meets real resistance, discouraging an animal from getting at the seed while it is still developing.

options.label: The spikes help the husk float if it lands in water
options.feedback: Sharp spikes projecting outward add drag and offer no trapped air, unlike the fibrous husk built specifically for floating, such as a coconut's.

options.label: The spikes are what allow the husk to photosynthesize
options.feedback: A husk of this kind is typically a dense, woody covering, not built to carry out photosynthesis, which is handled by the plant's leaves instead.

options.label: The spikes attach the husk to a passing animal's fur, the way a hooked burr does
options.feedback: This husk falls to the ground and splits open on its own rather than hitching a ride on fur, unlike a smaller hooked seed built specifically for that purpose.

items.ok_line: The spikes exist to keep the seed inside alone until it is ready.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to a hand, paw or mouth that closes around a husk covered in sharp points.
items.exp_title: A shell built to discourage, not to travel
items.exp_text: A husk covered in sharp spines is unpleasant and often painful for an animal to bite into or grip, which discourages it from reaching the seed while it is still developing inside. That armour is only temporary: once the seed inside is finally ready, the husk dries and splits open on its own, releasing it without the spines needing to be crossed again. Until that point, the spikes are simply doing the job of keeping the seed left alone.

items.prompt: Bramble and rose stems are lined with sharp thorns beneath the flower and fruit clusters they carry. What does that arrangement protect?

options.label: The thorns are simply left over from an older, unrelated function and no longer serve the plant
options.feedback: Thorns positioned so consistently along the exact stems that lead to flowers and fruit are too deliberate a pattern to be a leftover with no remaining purpose.

options.label: The thorny stem makes it harder for a browsing animal to reach the flowers or ripening fruit growing along it
options.feedback: An animal has to push past or around sharp thorns to reach the flowers and fruit sitting further along the same stem, which discourages many browsers from bothering at all.

options.label: Thorns release a scent that repels animals from a distance
options.feedback: A thorn is a rigid, sharp physical structure with nothing to release. It works purely by being difficult and painful to push past, not by any smell.

options.label: Thorns are there to catch spiderwebs that then trap insects harmful to the flowers
options.feedback: Whatever incidental webs end up caught on a thorny stem are not what the thorns exist for. Their placement along the stem leading to the flowers points to a much more direct role.

items.ok_line: Reaching the flowers means getting past the thorns first.
items.ko_line: The thorns line the very stem an animal would have to travel along to reach the flowers or fruit at the end of it.
items.exp_title: A barrier along the only approach
items.exp_text: A bramble or rose stem lined with sharp thorns forces any browsing animal to push through a genuinely painful obstacle to reach whatever grows further along it. Since the flowers and developing fruit sit at the end of that very stem, an animal deterred by the thorns never gets close enough to damage or eat them early. The thorns do not have to guard the flowers directly — guarding the only path toward them does the same job.

items.prompt: The seed pod of a plant like cowhage is covered in fine hairs that cause intense itching on contact. What does that irritation achieve for the plant?

options.label: The itching helps the hairs stick more firmly to fur for travel
options.feedback: The hairs cause a chemical reaction on skin rather than acting as hooks, and they detach and embed themselves rather than clinging on for a longer ride.

options.label: The itching signals to the plant that its pod has been touched
options.feedback: A plant has no way to sense or receive a signal back from an animal's reaction. Whatever the itching accomplishes happens entirely in the animal, not in the plant.

options.label: The itching softens the pod so it can be eaten more easily
options.feedback: The irritating hairs sit on the outside of the pod and have no effect on how tough or soft the pod's own tissue is underneath them.

options.label: The irritation discourages an animal from touching or handling the pod, protecting the developing seeds inside from being disturbed or eaten
options.feedback: An animal that brushes against the pod and feels the sharp itching quickly learns to avoid touching it again, leaving the seeds inside undisturbed.

items.ok_line: One unpleasant touch teaches an animal to stay away from the rest.
items.ko_line: Think about what an animal does the moment after it brushes against a pod covered in irritating hairs, and every time after that.
items.exp_title: A deterrent felt rather than tasted
items.exp_text: The fine hairs on a cowhage pod embed tiny irritant particles into skin on contact, causing sharp itching almost immediately. An animal that experiences that reaction once quickly learns to avoid touching the plant's pods again, without needing to bite into or damage them first. The seeds inside stay undisturbed simply because handling the pod at all has become something worth avoiding.

items.prompt: Some fruit pits, like a cherry stone, are hard enough that an animal's teeth cannot easily crush them while it eats the soft flesh around them. What does that hardness protect?

options.label: It shields the seed inside from being crushed by chewing, even while the flesh surrounding it is being eaten away
options.feedback: The animal's teeth can tear and chew through the soft flesh easily, but the hard stone resists that same pressure, so the embryo inside stays intact even as everything around it is consumed.

options.label: It keeps the flesh from spoiling while still attached to the pit
options.feedback: The pit's hardness does nothing to slow the flesh's own ripening or spoiling. What it is resisting is mechanical pressure, from teeth, not decay.

options.label: It stops the seed from absorbing too much sugar from the flesh around it
options.feedback: A seed's connection to the surrounding flesh is not about limiting how much sugar reaches it; the hard pit's role is purely mechanical protection against being crushed.

options.label: It makes the fruit float if it falls into water
options.feedback: A dense, solid pit like this is generally too heavy on its own to provide meaningful buoyancy, unlike a husk specifically built with trapped air for floating.

items.ok_title: Safe inside a shell that will not give
items.ok_line: Everything around the pit can be eaten. The pit itself does not have to yield.
items.ko_line: An animal's teeth easily tear through the soft flesh around the pit. What is the pit's hardness resisting that the flesh is not?
items.exp_title: A shell hard enough to survive the meal
items.exp_text: The soft flesh of a fruit like a cherry offers no resistance to chewing, but the stone at its centre is built dense and hard enough that ordinary bite pressure cannot crush it. An animal can eat all of the flesh surrounding the pit, or even swallow the pit whole, without the embryo sealed inside ever being damaged by that chewing. The seed survives the very meal that is meant to carry it away.

items.prompt: In a plant like the Chinese lantern, the flower's sepals grow into a papery case that encloses the developing fruit inside. What does that case do while the fruit is still forming?

options.label: It photosynthesizes to feed the fruit growing inside it
options.feedback: A thin, papery casing like this is built mainly as a covering rather than as a working leaf, and the fruit inside continues to be fed through its own connection to the plant.

options.label: It collects rainwater to keep the fruit from drying out
options.feedback: The papery case is loosely wrapped and open enough that it does not hold standing water, and the fruit's own skin is what manages its water content.

options.label: It shields the developing fruit from insects and other small threats while it is still vulnerable and unripe
options.feedback: Growing fully around the fruit like a shell, the papery case makes it much harder for a small insect to reach and damage the fruit before it has finished developing.

options.label: It attracts pollinators to finish fertilizing the flower after the case has formed
options.feedback: By the time this case has grown around the fruit, fertilization has already happened and the flower's petals are gone; there is nothing left at this stage for a pollinator to visit.

items.ok_title: A shell grown from spare parts
items.ok_line: Sepals that had already done their first job are put to a second one.
items.ko_line: The case forms only after the flower's job of attracting a pollinator is already finished. What could it be protecting during the stage that follows?
items.exp_text: The sepals that once protected the unopened flower bud do not simply fall away after pollination in this plant; instead they keep growing, expanding into a loose papery case that wraps fully around the fruit developing inside it. That case acts as a physical barrier, making it far harder for a small insect or other threat to reach and damage the fruit while it is still unripe and vulnerable. Only once the fruit inside has matured does the case usually dry and open, exposing what it spent the whole time shielding.

items.prompt: Some trees and shrubs produce an enormous crop of seeds all in the same year, after several years of producing very little. How does that pattern help more seeds survive being eaten?

options.label: The seed-eating animals leave the area entirely in the years with a heavy crop
options.feedback: A large, sudden crop of seeds is exactly what draws seed-eating animals in and keeps them feeding nearby, rather than driving them away.

options.label: Producing far more seeds than the local seed-eating animals can possibly eat in that one season leaves a surplus that survives simply because the animals run out of appetite before the seeds run out
options.feedback: Even well-fed seed-eating animals reach a limit to how much they can eat in a season, and once a crop is large enough to exceed that limit, everything beyond it survives untouched purely because there was too much of it to finish.

options.label: The seeds produced in a heavy year are less nutritious, so animals prefer not to eat them
options.feedback: A large seed crop is not made deliberately less appealing or nutritious. The surviving surplus comes from sheer quantity outpacing appetite, not from animals choosing to avoid it.

options.label: Skipping most years lets the plant build up a poison that only appears during the heavy year
options.feedback: The pattern here works through overwhelming quantity, not through a toxin appearing only in certain years. The seeds themselves are not chemically different in a heavy year.

items.ok_line: The surplus survives simply because appetite has a limit and the crop does not respect it.
items.ko_line: A seed-eating animal can only eat so much in one season, no matter how much food is available. What happens to whatever is left once that limit is reached?
items.exp_text: Seed-eating animals can only eat so much in a single season, and their numbers are usually kept in check by the small, steady crops produced in most years. When a plant instead produces an unusually enormous crop all at once, the local animals reach the limit of how much they can possibly eat long before the seeds themselves run out. Whatever is left over once that appetite is exhausted survives simply because there was too much of it to finish in time.

items.prompt: A plant sometimes drops a fruit to the ground while it is still unripe, especially one that shows signs of being attacked by a pest. Why let go of it early?

options.label: Dropping the fruit early can cut off a pest developing inside it before it can finish its life cycle and spread to other fruit still on the plant
options.feedback: A pest growing inside a fruit still attached to the plant has a direct route to spread once it matures, so sacrificing that one fruit early can stop it before it ever reaches the rest of the crop.

options.label: Unripe fruit is dropped to make room for new flowers to open in its place
options.feedback: A single dropped fruit does not free up space for an entirely new flower to grow in its exact spot, and this response happens specifically when a fruit shows signs of attack, not as routine thinning.

options.label: Dropping early lets the fruit finish ripening faster once it is on the ground
options.feedback: A fruit separated early from the plant loses its supply of water and nutrients rather than gaining anything that would speed up ripening once it has fallen.

options.label: It is a random event with no benefit to the plant, caused simply by the fruit's own weight
options.feedback: This dropping happens specifically and consistently when a fruit shows signs of being attacked, well beyond what its weight alone would explain, which points to a deliberate response rather than an accident.

items.ok_line: One fruit sacrificed can be cheaper than an infestation left to spread.
items.ko_line: A pest developing inside one fruit that stays attached to the plant has an easy route to reach every other fruit nearby. What does removing that one fruit early prevent?
items.exp_title: Sacrificing one fruit to protect the rest
items.exp_text: A pest that has begun developing inside a fruit still attached to the plant is in a good position to finish growing there and then spread to other fruit growing nearby. By dropping that particular fruit to the ground early, the plant removes the pest's food source and its route to the rest of the crop before it can complete that spread. The loss of one unripe fruit early is smaller than the loss the plant would face if the pest were left to finish developing.

items.prompt: Some fruits carry more bitter, defensive chemicals in their skin than in the soft flesh just beneath it. Why concentrate the defence there?

options.label: The skin needs the chemicals to stay a bright colour
options.feedback: A fruit's colour comes from separate pigment compounds, not from the bitter chemicals meant to deter early feeding, and the two are not linked in this way.

options.label: Chemicals collect in the skin only as a by-product of ripening, with no particular purpose
options.feedback: These defensive compounds are found concentrated in the skin at a level well beyond what would appear as a simple leftover from ripening, pointing to a deliberate placement rather than an accident.

options.label: The skin absorbs chemicals from the soil that the flesh underneath cannot reach
options.feedback: A fruit's skin and the flesh beneath it are both fed through the same connection to the rest of the plant, so the skin has no separate route to soil chemicals that the flesh lacks.

options.label: The skin is the first thing a small chewing animal or insect bites into, so putting the strongest defence there deters an attack before real damage reaches the edible flesh underneath
options.feedback: A small animal or insect testing the fruit meets the strongest, most bitter defence right at first contact, often discouraging it before it ever bites through to the flesh the plant wants a larger animal to eat and disperse instead.

items.ok_line: Whatever touches the fruit first meets the strongest defence first.
items.ko_line: Think about which part of the fruit any small chewing animal or insect actually reaches first, before it can get anywhere near the flesh underneath.
items.exp_title: Defence placed at the point of first contact
items.exp_text: A small chewing animal or insect testing a fruit for the first time makes contact with the skin before it can reach anything underneath it. By concentrating bitter, defensive compounds specifically in that outer layer, the plant discourages that early, damaging contact right at the first bite, often before the attacker gets any further. The flesh beneath stays comparatively mild, since it is meant to be eaten whole later by the larger animal the plant relies on to carry its seeds away.

items.prompt: Some seeds contain a toxin that is unpleasant or mildly harmful in a small amount but rarely kills the animal that eats a few of them. Why not make the toxin strong enough to be fatal?

options.label: A stronger toxin would be too costly for the plant to produce in any amount
options.feedback: Plants regularly produce far more potent toxins elsewhere in nature when the situation calls for it, so cost alone does not explain why this particular toxin is kept mild.

options.label: A mild dose teaches the animal to avoid that plant's seeds afterward, while a fatal one would remove the very animal the plant may still rely on to disperse its other seeds
options.feedback: An animal that survives an unpleasant, non-lethal experience learns to avoid those seeds in the future, while a toxin strong enough to kill would also destroy any usefulness that animal might have had in carrying the plant's seeds elsewhere.

options.label: A mild toxin is easier for the seed to store without damaging itself
options.feedback: The strength of a toxin and how safely a seed can store it are not directly linked in this way; the seed's own tissue is generally unharmed by a much stronger toxin as well.

options.label: The toxin only becomes fatal once the seed has already germinated
options.feedback: A germinating seed is expending its stored toxin, if anything, rather than gaining new strength, so a toxin does not become more dangerous at that later stage.

items.ok_line: A lesson the animal survives is more useful to the plant than one it does not.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to an animal that dies from eating a seed, versus one that simply learns from an unpleasant experience and lives.
items.exp_title: A deterrent that needs its target alive
items.exp_text: An animal that eats a few seeds and experiences a mild, unpleasant reaction survives the encounter and learns from it, becoming less likely to eat that plant's seeds again in the future. A toxin strong enough to kill outright would remove that same animal permanently, along with any future usefulness it might have had for the plant, including as an occasional disperser of the same seeds elsewhere. Keeping the dose sublethal turns the animal into a lesson learned rather than a loss with no return.
